newsitem.title: USA: Big retailers report disappointing earnings.
newsitem.headline: Big retailers report disappointing earnings.

text.p: Retail giants Wal-Mart Stores Inc. and J.C. Penney Co. posted disappointing profits Tuesday as concern about the coming holiday shopping season took its toll on the stock prices of major store chains.

Wal-Mart, the nation's largest retailer, earned $684.0 million, or 30 cents a share, in the third quarter, up from $612.0 million, or 27 cents a share, a year earlier. Sales rose 12 percent to $25.6 billion in the quarter.

The results were weaker than the consensus Wall Street estimate of 31 cents a share, according to the First Call service, which tracks analyst forecasts. Wal-Mart's stock closed down $1.25 at $25.25 on the New York Stock Exchange.
The stocks of several other large retailers fell despite upbeat remarks by Wal-Mart and other chains about Christmas.

"The company is well positioned for the holiday season, and we have an excellent opportunity to reach our goals for the fourth quarter and the year," Wal-Mart President David Glass said in a statement.

Wall Street analysts, however, were a bit more cautious about the key holiday season. While many stores have been careful to stock less inventory this year to avoid profit-eating clearance sales, they have five fewer days from Thanksgiving and Dec. 25 to tempt customers to buy.
"It will have the tendency to reduce impulse sales," said Steven Schuster of First Manhattan Co. "While it won't be a barn burner, holiday sales should be respectable."

J.C. Penney, the nation's fifth-largest retailer, said it earned $236 million, or 95 cents a share, during the third quarter. A year earlier, it earned $240 million, or 95 cents a share. Sales rose 8 percent to $5.5 billion.

The results included expenses for the integration of Fay's Inc. drug stores, which Penney bought for $285 million earlier this year. Without those non-recurring expenses, Penney would have earned $257 million, or $1.03 a share, which was in line with analysts' estimates.
While sales were strong, Penney said results were hurt by a seven-cent-a-share cost for bad credit card debt following a huge wave of delinquencies and bankruptcies by U.S. consumers.
Promotions aimed at boosting sales of new lines of more fashionable women's apparel and other merchandise also put a drag on Penney's margins.
Penney's stock fell 50 cents to $52 on the New York Stock Exchange.

Analysts said investors are worried that Penney's effort to become a bigger player in the drugstore industry will hurt profits over the long run. Earlier this month, Penney announced plans to buy Eckerd Corp. for $2.5 billion in cash and stock, its third pharmacy acqisition in a year and a half.
Sales from the drugstore operation, which is becoming a bigger share of Penney's total volume, bring lower profits per sale than do clothing transactions.

But supporters of Penney's expansion strategy note that while drugstore sales have lower profits, expenses are lower in that business. Besides, Penney has few options for growth due to saturation in the department store industry.
"It's a matter of maximizing an existing asset," said Schuster of First Manhattan. "There's no reason to believe" it won't pay off.

Atlanta-based Home Depot Inc. said its profits increased to $221 million, or 46 cents a share, during the third quarter from $175 million, or 37 cents a share, a year earlier. Sales rose 23 percent to $4.9 billion.

Home Depot's stock fell $3.375 to $53.375 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the largest net loss leader. While the home improvement retail giant's earnings met Wall Street estimates, analysts said the stock dropped on disappointment that its profits did not increase more robustly.
Last week, the market grew jittery about Home Depot's performance after competitor Lowe's Co. Inc. said its fourth-quarter earnings would be below expectations.
Home Depot, whose shares fell in reaction to Lowe's comments, responded with a statement that it was comfortable with Wall Street estimates for its third-quarter and full-year results.

The statement ignited hopes Home Depot's profits might be stronger than expected for the third quarter, analysts said. "I think because they said that, people were looking for them to beat the number," said Alan Rifkin of Dain Bosworth.
